evidence_quotes.quote: By combining previously scattered historical, legal, and ethnographic sources, this article examines Australian Aboriginal dam and weir construction along the Roper River, focusing on the repeated re-purposing, re-contextualization and reinterpretation of the structures over time by both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal protagonists.

The act of placing paperbark and bush timber into braided channels in the upper Roper has had multiple purposes: Aboriginal subsistence, drinking water for cattle, ﬂood irrigation, wetland management, erosion control, and directing water to downstream users.

evidence_quotes.quote: Now focused entirely on events in 1945, the issues outlined by Lyons were: the factual question of whether Holt’s downstream cattle losses in 1945 were due to the weirs (as Holt claimed) or to poor feed availability and his failure to employ Aboriginal labour to extract bogged cattle (as the Elsey defendants claimed); the validity of the permits provided to Elsey by the Administrator; and whether the dams constituted illegal ‘obstructions’ rather than legal ‘diversions’.

evidence_quotes.quote: The research data were obtained through a combination of archival searches, ﬁeld interviews, and participant observation.

Holt took the matter to court in 1946, and the judge (Justice Wells) found in his favour and banned the practice. Despite the ban, Aboriginal cattle workers continued to construct similar structures elsewhere in the area until the 1970s, particularly on the adjacent Moroak Station.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper examines historical and contemporary Aboriginal construction of temporary wooden-pole and paperbark dams/weirs in braided channels of the upper Roper River for subsistence fishing and wildfowl hunting, cattle watering, pasture flood irrigation, wetland management, and erosion control. It does not examine household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 alone because it examines legal, administrative, and judicial water-governance factors—specifically British-derived common-law riparian doctrine, surface-water diversion permits issued by the Administrator of the Northern Territory under the 1938 Water Ordinance, police inspections/removals, and the 1946 Northern Territory Supreme Court injunction outlawing the Red Lily Lagoon weirs (even under the plain reading, however, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper fails Criteria 1 and 4). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, c2_legal_admin_factor is 'no' because those legal and permitting rules govern in-stream surface-water river diversions for subsistence fishing, pastoral livestock watering/irrigation, and erosion control rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Empirical qualitative historical, archival socio-legal, and ethnographic case study combining court transcripts and judgments (1946 Northern Territory Supreme Court), government archives, station correspondence, participant observation, and formal interviews with 18 Aboriginal participants and 1 non-Aboriginal former pastoralist across five field trips.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes concern the construction, prohibition, geographic relocation, and repurposing of in-stream river channel weirs (for fish/fowl harvesting, preventing cattle bogging, pasture flood irrigation, and channel erosion control) and anthropological interpretations of Aboriginal autonomy and intercultural relations—not household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Within its own natural-resource scope, the study clearly identifies the study design (archival-ethnographic historical case study), population and setting (Mangarrayi and Yangman Aboriginal groups and pastoralists in the upper Roper River catchment, Northern Territory, Australia; 19 interviewees plus historical/court archives from 1908–2011), legal/colonial exposures, and river-management outcomes.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English (with a French abstract at the end).

study_design: Qualitative historical-ethnographic and archival socio-legal case study
population_and_sample: Mangarrayi and Yangman Aboriginal communities and non-Aboriginal pastoralists in the upper Roper River catchment (Elsey, Roper Valley, and Moroak Stations), Northern Territory, Australia; formal interviews with 18 Aboriginal people and 1 non-Aboriginal former pastoralist across five field trips plus archival and court records (1908–2011)
exposure: Colonial pastoralism, Northern Territory 1938 Water Ordinance diversion permits, police inspections, and 1946 Supreme Court common-law riparian litigation and injunction against river damming
outcome: Prohibition of Red Lily Lagoon weirs, subsequent covert relocation and continuation of river weirs on Moroak Station (1950s–1970s) and revival on Elsey Station (2010), and shifting multi-valent interpretations of Aboriginal water resource management
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; specifically Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). This anthropological and environmental-legal history examines in-stream river channel weir construction by Aboriginal people and pastoralists along the upper Roper River for subsistence fishing/wildfowl hunting, watering cattle to prevent bogging, flood irrigation of pasture, wetland management, and riverbank erosion control. Although it empirically analyses legal and regulatory interventions (permits under the 1938 Water Ordinance and a 1946 Supreme Court riparian-law injunction), those rules concern surface-water river diversion for fisheries, pastoralism, and land management rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access; accordingly, it fails Criteria 1, 2 (narrow rule-type service-access reading), and 4, and is excluded under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
